01.n: Abbott-Smith explains it as properly an imperative of ὁράω, 'see', used as a pointing particle, much more often in the Septuagint and New Testament than in classical Greek.

02.r: The wage owed for the harvest.

03.r: The pay owed for the harvest work.
03.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse under the proper sense, 'wages, hire'. The YLT's 'reward' loses the sense of pay.

04.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case.

05.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'a field labourer, husbandman', and he lists this verse there, together with Matthew 20:2.

06.r: With the participle, describes the labourers.

07.r: They cut the grain in the owners' fields.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to reap', and this is its only New Testament use. This study writes 'mowed', with the ASV and BSB, to keep it apart from θερίζω, 'reap', later in the verse.

09.n: The ordinary word for land or country, the first senses in Abbott-Smith's entry; here, in the plural, the fields the labourers worked.

11.r: The article attaches the next phrase to 'the wage'.

s: has been kept back by fraud
12.r: The wage was never paid: the workers were cheated of it.
12.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to defraud, deprive of, despoil', and notes that in classical Greek it was used chiefly of misappropriating trust funds. In the Septuagint it stands at Deuteronomy 24:14 for Hebrew עָשַׁק, in the law on the hired worker's pay. A perfect participle: the wrong was done and still stands.
t: by fraud has been kept back

13.n: Literally 'from you'. With the passive verb, the translations take it as naming the agent, 'by you'.

15.r: The unpaid wage itself cries out, as if it had a voice.
15.n: Abbott-Smith calls the word properly imitative, of the raven's croak, and so of inarticulate cries: to scream, cry out. He also records a use 'of crying for vengeance', which fits this verse, though that is a reading, not a listing shown for it.

18.n: Abbott-Smith gives simply 'a cry', with this verse its only New Testament use. The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew זְעָקָה, outcry.

19.r: With the participle, the workers again.

20.r: The same labourers, now named as reapers.
20.n: The ordinary verb for reaping, the same as 'reaping' in Matthew 25:24. Abbott-Smith lists this verse under its literal sense.

23.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse for the phrase with 'enter', εἰσέρχεσθαι: cries that enter the ears.

24.n: No article in the Greek, as often with this word for God; English needs 'the'.

25.r: A Hebrew title of God: Lord of hosts.
25.n: A Hebrew word kept untranslated in the Greek. Abbott-Smith explains it as 'hosts or armies', and notes that the Septuagint keeps it chiefly in Isaiah, elsewhere translating the phrase as κύριος παντοκράτωρ, 'Lord Almighty', or κύριος τῶν δυνάμεων, 'Lord of the powers'.

26.n: A perfect: the cries have entered and are now heard.
